title: The Conditions of Rebirth
author: Annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: (Original text from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu)

inline.s: Original text from the Posthumous Collection of Master Chewu

The conditions of rebirth: Every thought we raise is a condition for receiving birth in a future life. Carefully examine the thoughts you raise in daily life, and see with which of the ten dharma-realms they correspond most often, and with which they correspond most intensely; then you will know clearly which dharma-realm you will be reborn into in your next life and what your circumstances will be — without needing to ask anyone else.

[Ten dharma-realms] The hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, heavens, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas. The first six are the six ordinary realms; the last four are the four holy realms.

[This present single thought of our mind — wholly true it becomes false, and wholly false it is true; all day long it does not change, and all day long it follows conditions. If it does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm and recollect the Buddha-realm, it will recollect the other nine realms; if it does not recollect the three vehicles, it recollects the six ordinary realms; if it does not recollect humans and heavens, it recollects the three evil paths; if it does not recollect ghosts and animals, it recollects the hells. For as long as there is a mind, there cannot be no thought. The thoughtless essence of mind is realized only by the Buddha alone. From the stage of virtual enlightenment (dengjue) on down, all still have thoughts. Every thought that arises must fall within the ten realms, and no thought arises outside the ten realms — because there is nothing outside the ten dharma-realms.]

Our present single thought is either a false mind or a true mind; the essence of the mind does not change all day long, yet the state of the mind’s delusion or awakening changes all day long according to what it conditions and recollects. If it does not follow the conditions of the Buddha-realm and recollect the Buddha-realm, it conditions and recollects the other nine realms. Among these nine realms, if it does not condition and recollect the three vehicles (śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, bodhisattva), it conditions and recollects the six ordinary realms (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans, heavens). Among the six ordinary realms, if it does not condition and recollect humans and heavens, it conditions and recollects the three evil paths (hells, hungry ghosts, animals). Among the three evil paths, if it does not condition and recollect ghosts and animals, it conditions and recollects the hells. All this is because, as long as there is a mind, there cannot be no thought. The entirely thoughtless essence of the mind is realized only by the Buddha. From the stage of the virtual-enlightenment (dengjue) bodhisattva on down, all still have thoughts. Therefore, every thought that arises is necessarily a recollection of one of the ten dharma-realms, because the ten dharma-realms already encompass everything.

[Wholly true it becomes false, wholly false it is true] The present single thought has two states, true and false: when the self-nature is in charge, it is true; when habit-energy is in charge, it is false. “Wholly true it becomes false, wholly false it is true” means the true and the false cannot coexist — it is either wholly true or wholly false. With a single thought of delusion, the entire true mind becomes a false mind (wholly true it becomes false); with a single thought of awakening, the entire false mind becomes the true mind (wholly false it is true). Here “true” means original — the true mind is the mind’s original state; “false” is the false of false movement, meaning disorder. When the original state is muddied and disordered by false movement, the true mind becomes a false mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “When the preceding thought is deluded, one is an ordinary person; when the following thought is awakened, one is a Buddha.” [All day long it does not change, all day long it follows conditions] Although the mind has the distinction of delusion and awakening — when deluded it is wholly true becoming false, when awakened wholly false becoming true — the essence of the mind (the self-nature) undergoes no change whatsoever (neither arising nor ceasing, neither increasing nor decreasing); hence it is said: “All day long it does not change, all day long it follows conditions; all day long it follows conditions, all day long it does not change.” [Virtual-enlightenment bodhisattva] Among the fifty-two stages of the Mahāyāna, the fifty-first is called dengjue, “virtual enlightenment” — this is a bodhisattva about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s, hence the name “virtual enlightenment.” The fifty-second stage is Buddhahood.
[Every thought that arises is a condition for receiving birth. Truly, one who understands this principle and yet does not practice Buddha-recitation has never existed.]
Every thought we raise is a condition for receiving birth in a future life. One who truly understands this principle and yet does not practice Buddha-recitation — there is no such person.

[If this mind can correspond with the Buddha’s equanimity, great loving-kindness and compassion, the merits of his environment and person, and the great name of myriad virtues, then it is recollecting the Buddha-realm. If it can correspond with the bodhi mind and the myriad practices of the six perfections, then it is recollecting the bodhisattva-realm. If, with the mind of selflessness, it corresponds with the twelve links of dependent origination, then it is recollecting the pratyekabuddha-realm. If, with the mind of selflessness, it contemplates the four noble truths, then it is recollecting the śrāvaka-realm.]

If this thought of the mind can correspond with the Buddha’s equanimity, great loving-kindness and compassion, the merits of his environment and person, and the great name of myriad virtues, then one is recollecting the Buddha-realm; if it can correspond with the bodhi mind and the myriad practices of the six perfections, one is recollecting the bodhisattva-realm; if, with the mind of selflessness, it corresponds with the twelve links of dependent origination, one is recollecting the pratyekabuddha-realm; if, with the mind of selflessness, it contemplates the four noble truths, one is recollecting the śrāvaka-realm.

[Environment and person] The circumstantial retribution and the direct retribution. The world’s lands, houses, utensils, and the like, which the body relies upon, are called the “circumstantial retribution” (yibao); the sentient being’s body, a provisional combination of the five aggregates, which is the result of past karma, is called the “direct retribution” (zhengbao).

[Or if it corresponds with the four dhyānas and the eight concentrations, as well as the superior grade of the ten good deeds, then it is recollecting the heaven-realm. If it corresponds with the five precepts, it is recollecting the human-realm. If one practices the precepts and good deeds while harboring a mind of anger, arrogance, and rivalry, one falls into the asura-realm.]

If this thought of the mind corresponds with the four dhyānas and eight concentrations, as well as the superior ten good deeds, one is recollecting the heaven-realm; if it corresponds with the five precepts, one is recollecting the human-realm; if one practices the five precepts and ten good deeds while harboring a mind of anger, envy, arrogance, and rivalry, one is recollecting the asura-realm.

[Four dhyānas and eight concentrations] The four dhyānas are the four meditative absorptions of the form realm; the eight concentrations are the four dhyānas of the form realm and the four formless concentrations of the formless realm. [Ten good deeds] The ten kinds of good karma, namely: not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, not speaking divisively, not speaking harshly, not speaking frivolously, not being greedy, not being angry, and not being deluded. [Five precepts] Not killing, not stealing, not committing sexual misconduct, not lying, and not taking intoxicants. Not killing means not taking the life of any living creature; not stealing means not taking the property of others; not committing sexual misconduct means not engaging in sexual relations outside of marriage; not lying means not speaking deceitful words; not taking intoxicants means not consuming alcoholic drinks or drugs that stupefy the mind.
[If with a gentle, mild
(ruǎn, “soft”)

mind one recollects the inferior grade of the ten evils, one falls into the animal-realm. If with a mind half gentle and half intense one corresponds with the middle grade of the ten evils, one falls into the hungry-ghost-realm. If with a fierce, blazing mind one corresponds with the superior grade of the ten evils, one falls into the hell-realm. The ten evils are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and wrong views; the reverse of these are the ten good deeds.]

If with a gentle (not intense) mind one recollects the mild ten evils, one is recollecting the animal-realm. If with a somewhat intense mind one corresponds with the middling ten evils, one is recollecting the hungry-ghost-realm. If with a very intense (fierce, urgent, blazing) mind one corresponds with the worst ten evils, one is recollecting the hell-realm. The ten evils are killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, frivolous speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and delusion; their reverse are the ten good deeds.

[One should secretly examine the thoughts that arise in daily life, and see with which realm they correspond most often and with which they correspond most intensely; then as for the place where one will settle one’s body and establish one’s life in days to come, one need not trouble to ask anyone else.]

One should carefully examine the thoughts that arise in daily life, and see with which of the ten dharma-realms they correspond most often and with which they correspond most intensely; then as for which dharma-realm one will be reborn into in the next life and what one’s circumstances will be (the place to settle one’s body and establish one’s life), one need not ask anyone else — it will be perfectly clear.
[Secretly] Carefully, minutely.

Carefully examine the thoughts that arise in daily life, and see with which of the ten dharma-realms they correspond most often and with which they correspond most intensely — this is the place of self-examination! Therefore, the work of practice must be done where thoughts arise and the mind moves.
